title: Manage the utilisation of a poultry site or farm, at

lessons.title: Planning site capacity and placement schedules
lessons.html:
Getting the most from fixed assets

Poultry houses, equipment, water and electricity are expensive fixed assets. Every day a house stands empty without a good reason is lost income. Site utilisation means planning so that houses are full for as much of the year as is safe and sustainable, without overcrowding birds or skipping the rest periods that biosecurity needs.

Understanding capacity

The capacity of a house depends on floor area, the stocking density recommended for the bird type and the climate control the house can provide. An open-sided house in the Limpopo lowveld cannot carry the same summer density as a closed, tunnel-ventilated house. Capacity is also limited by feeder and drinker space, ventilation capacity, the size of the generator and the water supply. Animal welfare codes and customer specifications may set maximum densities, so check the requirements that apply to your operation.

The production cycle

For broilers, a cycle includes placement, the grow-out period, depletion, cleaning and disinfection, and a down time before the next placement. For layers it covers the laying cycle, depletion, cleaning and pullet transfer. The total cycle length determines how many batches a house can produce per year.

Building a placement schedule

  1. List every house with its capacity and type.
  2. Fix the cleaning and down time needed between flocks.
  3. Stagger placements so that catching crews, feed deliveries, abattoir slots and labour are spread evenly.
  4. Confirm chick or pullet orders with the hatchery well in advance.
  5. Check that feed mill, transport and market can absorb the planned output.

Consider whether the site should run all-in all-out, with every house on the site at the same age, or multi-age. All-in all-out is far better for biosecurity because the whole site can be emptied and cleaned, breaking disease cycles. Multi-age sites keep labour and cash flow steadier but carry higher disease risk.

Measuring utilisation

Track house occupancy as days with birds divided by days available, and output per square metre per year. Compare these across houses and years to see where time is being lost, for example slow cleaning, late chick delivery or equipment breakdowns.

lessons.title: Managing land, water, waste and site resources
lessons.html:
The whole site, not just the houses

A poultry farm uses more than its houses. Roads, feed silos, the water source and reservoirs, generators, staff facilities, mortality disposal areas, manure storage and surrounding land all have to be planned and managed so that they support production and comply with the law.

Water

Birds need clean water every hour of every day. Know your daily requirement at peak and make sure borehole yield, storage and reticulation can supply it with a reserve for power failures and fires. Water use from boreholes and rivers is regulated under the National Water Act 36 of 1998; confirm your use is lawful and keep meter readings. Test water quality regularly for bacteria and minerals and clean lines between flocks.

Energy

Load shedding has made backup power essential. Size generators for the full ventilation and lighting load, keep fuel stocks, test start them weekly under load and keep a log. Solar systems with batteries can lower costs but must still carry critical loads.

Manure, litter and mortalities

Spent litter and manure are a resource. They can be sold or composted and spread on crop land, which returns nutrients and can earn income. Store them away from houses and water sources, cover them to limit flies and runoff, and plan where they go. Mortalities must be disposed of by an approved method such as incineration, composting or a correctly built disposal pit, located away from water and the production area.

Land and layout

Keep a clean zone around houses with short grass and no rubbish to discourage rodents and wild birds. Separate clean and dirty traffic routes so that feed trucks do not cross manure or mortality routes. When planning new houses, allow distance between houses and between farms, and think about access roads in the rainy season. Under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 you are expected to prevent erosion and protect land and water resources around the site.

Reviewing utilisation

Once a year, review the site plan with your team: capacity used, bottlenecks, costs per unit of output and planned improvements. Present options to owners with costs in rand and the expected return.

Key points

  • Plan placements so houses stay productive while keeping proper cleaning and down time.
  • All-in all-out management lowers disease risk.
  • Water, power, litter and mortalities must be planned as part of the site.
  • Keep clean and dirty routes separate on the site.
  • Measure occupancy and output per square metre to find lost time.
